title: Inattentive ADHD in Adults: Symptoms
summary: Inattentive ADHD often goes unnoticed for decades. Learn the adult symptoms, how many you need to meet criteria, and what a real evaluation involves.
body_markdown:
Having trouble keeping your attention focused? Or struggling to stay organized and on top of your tasks, while your peers seem to have a handle on their lives? You may be one of the 6% of U.S. adults with ADHD.


This type of ADHD rarely presents through hyperactivity. You may never have disrupted a classroom in your youth, or a meeting in your adult life. But that doesn’t mean everything’s fine. Many adults with undiagnosed ADHD have navigated their lives thinking they may just be naturally careless or scatter-brained.


[The CDC estimates that 15.5 million U.S. adults have a current ADHD diagnosis.](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/wr/mm7340a1.htm) Of those adults, 55.9% were diagnosed after they turned 18.


## Inattentive ADHD at a glance


- **Clinical name:**[ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519712/table/ch3.t3/) (DSM-5-TR)
- **Adult threshold:** 5 or more of 9 inattention criteria, versus 6 for children under 17
- **Onset requirement:** several symptoms present before age 12, even when the diagnosis comes at 40
- **Settings requirement:** symptoms appear in two or more settings, usually work and home
- **Why adults miss it:** it rarely produces the disruptive behavior that triggers a childhood referral


## The three types of ADHD, compared


Inattentive ADHD sits inside ADHD. It’s not a separate diagnosis. The DSM-5-TR describes ADHD as one condition with three presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive, and combined. A provider assigns one of the three presentations based on which symptoms are observed to be dominant in a patient right now.


The way your ADHD presents is not permanent. Your symptoms and presentations can change throughout your life. If you had an ADHD diagnosis when you were a child, you can be diagnosed with a different type of ADHD as an adult.


### Types of ADHD: Inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive and combined


ADHD has 18 general symptoms, 9 of which describe inattention while the other nine describe hyperactivity-impulsivity.


What separates the types of ADHD is how many symptoms fall into each group.


Predominantly inattentive Predominantly hyperactive-impulsive Combined presentation


**Criteria met (age 17+)** 5+ of 9 inattention symptoms, fewer than 5 hyperactive-impulsive 5+ of 9 hyperactive-impulsive symptoms, fewer than 5 inattention 5+ in both groups


**How it reads to other people** Distracted, disorganized, hard to reach Restless, interrupting, impatient Both, in varying mixes


**How it’s usually caught in childhood** Often missed, since grades can hold up for years Caught early, because it disrupts a classroom Usually caught, driven by the visible half


**Common adult experience** Drifting attention, unfinished tasks, internal restlessness Talking over people, impulsive decisions, physical restlessness Attention and impulse difficulties together


**Frequency in adults** The most frequent presentation in older adolescents and adults Becomes less common with age, as hyperactive symptoms tend to decline Common, though it often trends toward inattentive over time


#### Predominantly inattentive presentation, often called ADHD inattentive type


This presentation covers sustained attention, working memory, and task initiation. Adults with predominantly inattentive ADHD can sit through a whole meeting while retaining almost nothing that was discussed.


#### Predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation


This presentation covers physical restlessness, interrupting, and acting before thinking things through. Most TV and film portrayals show this version of ADHD. That may be part of the reason why the other two types of ADHD often get overlooked.


#### Combined presentation


This presentation means that you meet the threshold in both types of ADHD at once. This type of ADHD is most often caught in childhood, because the hyperactive half gets noticed by teachers and parents.


ADHD presentations aren’t fixed for life.[A 2025 review in World Psychiatry found that hyperactive-impulsive symptoms decline more sharply with age](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12434367/) . Someone diagnosed with combined presentation ADHD at 8 years old may meet only the inattentive criteria at 30 years old.


## Inattentive ADHD symptoms in adults


At work, inattentive ADHD usually looks like unopened tasks, missed details and projects that stall at the planning stage. At home, it can look like unfinished chores and forgotten logistics.


DSM-5-TR inattention criterion What it can look like in an adult


Often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes Sending the invoice with the wrong figure after checking it twice


Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or activities Rereading the same paragraph of a contract and retaining none of it


Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly Your partner finishes a story and you realize you understood none of it


Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish duties in the workplace Ten projects started, two finished, none abandoned on purpose


Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities Missing a deadline you knew about, because you couldn’t sequence the steps


Often avoids or dislikes tasks requiring sustained mental effort Expense reports and tax forms sitting untouched for weeks


Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities Keys, wallet, badge, and the file you saved somewhere sensible


Is often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli One notification pulls you off task and you stay distracted for 40 minutes


Is often forgetful in daily activities Missed appointments, unreturned calls, a prescription never picked up


Adults 17 years and older need to present at least five of those nine symptoms to meet the criteria for inattentive ADHD. Children under 17 years old only need to meet six.


### What inattention looks like at work


The work setting tests your ability to start tasks and stay organized. Adults with inattentive ADHD often describe an inbox they can’t open or a project that stalls at the planning stage. Many of the same people perform well on anything urgent enough to force their focus.


Deadline-driven work can hide the difficulty for years. When a role changes to self-directed work with distant deadlines, a reliable employee with undiagnosed ADHD can start struggling.


### What inattention looks like at home


The home setting exposes challenges in your follow-through. Common examples include laundry that never leaves the machine and bills paid late despite the money being there. Partners often end up holding every appointment in their own head.


Some adults describe getting stuck at the start of a task they actively want to do.


### The internal experience


Inattentive ADHD can look calm on the outside, but the internal struggle can paint a different picture. Many adults report internal restlessness, or a sense of mental noise that never becomes visible fidgeting.


Many adults with undiagnosed ADHD report daydreaming, and they have a tendency to undersell the experience. What they usually mean is that their attention leaves without their permission and returns without warning, sometimes several times in just one conversation.


On the other hand, colleagues and partners can look at you and see a composed person. That’s why it’s so easy to overlook ADHD symptoms and challenges in undiagnosed adults.


## Why inattentive ADHD is missed in adults


Childhood screening for ADHD rarely begins with a screening tool. It begins with an adult who notices when a child is behaving disruptively.


A teacher who notices a child leaving their seat frequently may ask for an ADHD evaluation. But a child who just stares out the window rarely catches the attention of the teacher. Schools rarely flag the inattentive presentation of a child who may have ADHD.


Good grades add another layer of masking. Bright students with inattentive ADHD can perform well enough and not get flagged for ADHD. If the child gets average results, no one bothers to check if they spend four times longer on their homework than anyone else.


### Inattentive ADHD in women


Girls get referred for ADHD assessment far less often than boys.[In clinical samples, boys are diagnosed at 2 to 9 times the rate of girls.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4195638/) The same study reported that girls more often present with inattentive ADHD over hyperactive-impulsive symptoms.


[A 2025 study surveyed 28 women diagnosed in adulthood and found that their average age at diagnosis was 35.9 years,](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-04782-y) decades past the point where school screening could have caught it.


### Compensating until the compensations fail


Most adults with undiagnosed inattentive ADHD have built a system of workarounds that keeps anyone from asking deeper questions. They usually set up phone alarms for everything, or have a partner who handles scheduling, and have chosen jobs that have a solid external structure.


Those same workarounds are dependable until something in their life drastically changes. A promotion into self-managed work, or a new baby, or a manager who stops sending reminders can all remove the structures that adults with inattentive ADHD have long relied on. The symptoms that they were effectively managing can start causing visible problems.


By that time, there’s no teacher to start an ADHD referral, so you need to start it yourself. A few things can make that first conversation with a provider more productive:


1.


Write down symptoms you experience in two settings, not one. The ADHD criteria require symptoms in two or more settings, so bring examples from work and from home.


2.


Find any evidence or symptoms of ADHD from before age 12. Old report cards, a parent’s memory, or comments like “not working to potential” all count as part of your medical history.


3.


Bring situational examples, not just adjectives. “I missed three deadlines last quarter” tells a provider more than “I’m disorganized.”


4.


List the things you’ve already tried to deal with your challenges. Planners, apps and systems that failed all give your provider a clearer grasp of your struggles.


5.


Note anything that changed in your life recently. Sleep, stress, thyroid symptoms, and mood changes all belong in the same conversation.


Several common health conditions can also produce inattention that may look a great deal like ADHD, so it’s worth ruling those out first.


## Is it inattentive ADHD or something else?


Not all moments of disorganization point to inattentive ADHD. It might be something else, and a provider is the one who can tell. Inattention is a symptom, not a diagnosis, and several conditions can produce it.


Anxiety can consume your working memory, and your memory is what your attention depends on. Depression can slow your mental processing and flatten your motivation. Chronic short sleep and sleep apnea can cause daytime inattention on their own. An underactive thyroid can also cause brain fog and forgetfulness.


[Medical causes should be assessed before an ADHD diagnosis is confirmed.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12560001/) An ADHD evaluation helps rule those things out.


## How inattentive ADHD is diagnosed


Getting evaluated as an adult means a clinical conversation, not a score. Your provider reviews your current symptoms against the DSM-5-TR criteria. They also look for evidence of several symptoms before age 12, confirm impairment in two or more settings, and weigh those against other potential health conditions.


### What a comprehensive evaluation involves


-


An intake conversation covering current symptoms, work and home functioning, and what prompted the appointment.


-


A developmental history, including school experience and any records or family recollection from before age 12.


-


Standardized rating scales, used as one input to the clinical picture.


-


A review of medical and mental health history, including sleep, thyroid, mood, anxiety and current medications.


-


A diagnosis and personalized treatment plan tailored to your needs, when the criteria are met.


At Circle Medical, that process runs across a short series of video appointments. That gives your provider time to review your history between visits.[Our guide to getting diagnosed with ADHD online](https://www.circlemedical.com/blog-post/a-comprehensive-guide-to-getting-diagnosed-with-adhd-online) walks through what to expect.


### What an online test can and cannot tell you


An online inattentive ADHD test is a screener. It can tell you whether your symptoms resemble the criteria closely enough to be worth booking a full evaluation.


A screener can’t establish childhood onset, verify impairment across different settings, or rule out thyroid, sleep, and mood causes.


Online symptom screener Comprehensive evaluation


**What it produces** A score suggesting whether symptoms resemble ADHD A clinical determination against DSM-5-TR criteria


**Who reviews it** Usually an automated score A board-certified provider


**Checks onset before age 12** Rarely Yes


**Checks two or more settings** Rarely Yes


**Considers thyroid, sleep and mood causes** No Yes


**Can result in a diagnosis** No Yes, when the criteria are met


**Cost** Usually free Billed as a medical appointment

Once the evaluation is complete, treatment follows.


## Treatment options for inattentive ADHD


Behavioral strategies, therapy, and medication are the common treatment options for inattentive ADHD. These are the same treatments used for the other two ADHD presentations.


Behavioral strategies target the difficulties you’re having day-to-day. That can include externalizing task lists, breaking work into shorter blocks, and building structure that doesn’t depend on always having to remember things.


Therapy, particularly cognitive behavioral approaches adapted for ADHD, can address the avoidance and self-criticism that accumulate over undiagnosed decades.


Medication is a category your provider can discuss when it’s clinically appropriate, along with the tradeoffs and monitoring involved.


Which combination fits your case depends on your symptoms, your history, and your preferences. Our guide to[how ADHD is treated in adults](https://www.circlemedical.com/blog-post/how-to-treat-adhd-in-adults) covers the options in more depth.


## Common questions about inattentive ADHD in adults


### Is inattentive ADHD the same as ADD?


Effectively, yes. ADD was the older term for what the DSM-5-TR now calls ADHD predominantly inattentive presentation. The name changed as the diagnostic manuals were revised. ADD is no longer a current diagnosis, though it remains one of the most searched ADHD terms. A provider will assess you against the current criteria regardless of which term you use.


### Is inattentive ADHD a form of autism?


No. Inattentive ADHD and autism are separate diagnoses with separate criteria in the DSM-5-TR. They can co-occur, and the DSM-5 was the first edition to allow both diagnoses in the same person. Some difficulties do overlap, including attention regulation and social fatigue, so an evaluation that considers both can be worth asking about.


### Can you develop inattentive ADHD as an adult?


Under current criteria, no. The DSM-5-TR requires several symptoms to have been present before age 12, so ADHD isn’t something that begins in adulthood. What often happens is that lifelong symptoms only become impairing when adult demands increase. Our post on whether ADHD can appear later in life covers what late recognition looks like and how providers assess it.


### Can you have inattentive ADHD and still be successful at work?


Yes, and many adults do for years before seeking an evaluation. Success and impairment can exist together, particularly when someone compensates with long hours or a role that suits them. The criteria ask whether symptoms interfere with functioning, not whether you’ve failed at something. How much effort a job takes you is as relevant as the results it produces.


### How long does an ADHD evaluation take?


It varies by practice. Some evaluations happen in one long appointment. Others spread across a short series of shorter visits, which lets a provider review history and rating scales in between. At Circle Medical, ADHD evaluations typically run across a few video appointments. Ask any practice you’re considering how many visits their process involves before you book.


## What an inattentive ADHD diagnosis changes for adults


An ADHD diagnosis helps you understand your symptoms and gives you a roadmap on what you can do about them. Adults who are evaluated with ADHD in their thirties and forties can start to make sense of the ten years of unfinished projects. It becomes easier to understand that these things are not character flaws, but a condition with criteria and treatment options.


It also changes the treatment plans available to you. A diagnosis opens treatment options you can hash out with your provider. It also gives you language for a conversation with a manager or a partner that you’ve been putting off.
